draws.answer: [Ch. 1] A chief information officer (CIO) is the senior C-suite executive responsible for information technology within an organization; it is an internal-facing role. A CIO must possess deep knowledge of information technology and business processes—either alone is insufficient. CIOs direct the information technology organization, setting ongoing policies while also defining and executing significant initiatives under the direction of the CEO. CIOs often collaborate with data engineering leadership in organizations with a well-developed data culture. If an organization is not very high in its data maturity, a CIO will typically help shape its data culture. CIOs will work with engineers and architects to map out major initiatives and make strategic decisions on adopting major architectural elements, such as enterprise resource planning (ERP) and customer relationship management (CRM) systems, cloud migrations, data systems, and internal-facing IT. [Ch. 3] A data warehouse is a central data hub used for reporting and analysis; it contains data that is highly formatted and structured for analytics. items.note: ch07 'Practical Issues with Common File Formats'

draws.answer:
Files in [Ch. 5] are described as a sequence of bytes, typically stored on a disk. Applications often write data to files. Files may store local parameters, events, logs, images, and audio. In addition, files are a universal medium of data exchange. As much as data engineers wish that they could get data programmatically, much of the world still sends and receives files. For example, if you’re getting data from a government agency, there’s an excellent chance you’ll download the data as an Excel or CSV file or receive the file in an email. The main types of source file formats you’ll run into as a data engineer—files that originate either manually or as an output from a source system process—are Excel, CSV, TXT, JSON, and XML. These files have their quirks and can be structured (Excel, CSV), semistructured (JSON, XML, CSV), or unstructured (TXT, CSV). Although you’ll use certain formats heavily as a data engineer (such as Parquet, ORC, and Avro), we’ll cover these later and put the spotlight here on source system files. Chapter 6 covers the technical details of files. [Ch. 6] defines a file as a finite-length stream of bytes. We can append bytes to the file up to the limits of the host storage system. We can read from any location in the file or write updates to any location. Object storage behaves much like file storage but

Column-oriented databases store data in columns, allowing for faster query execution. Row-oriented databases organize data by rows. Columnar serialization in databases lets them read from only a subset of fields in one go, reducing query scan. Columnar databases do poorly for transactional queries but excel in scanning large amounts of data for analytics.

Column-oriented databases store data in columns, allowing for faster query execution. Row-oriented databases organize data by rows, which is common in transactional applications. Columnar databases are better for scanning large amounts of data, while row-based databases handle many queries quickly. Columnar storage lets you read only part of a row, reducing query time.

ETL stands for extract, transform, load. From [Ch. 3]. ELT, or extract, load, transform, is a data warehouse architecture where data is moved more or less directly from production systems into a staging area in the data warehouse. Staging in this setting indicates that the data is in a raw form. Rather than using an external system, transformations are handled directly in the data warehouse. The intention is to take advantage of the massive computational power of cloud data warehouses and data processing tools. Data is processed in batches, and transformed output is written into tables and views for analytics. Figure 3-11 shows the general process. ELT is also popular in a streaming arrangement, as events are streamed from a CDC process, stored in a staging area, and then subsequently transformed within the data warehouse. From [Ch. 3].

draws.asked_as: What is benefits of data meshs?
draws.answer:
In Chapter 9, a data mesh changes how teams serve data in an organization. Each domain team now handles two aspects: preparing data for apps, dashboards, and analytics, and running dashboards and analytics for their users. This shifts from siloed teams in Chapter 3. In Chapter 4, using a data mesh avoids unnecessary lock-in. Chapter 5 says data mesh and sharing go well together. Chapter 9 mentions teams in Chapter 5 share data.
Asked as: "What is benefits of data meshs?"

draws.asked_as: What is benefits of data meshs?
draws.answer:
[Ch. 9] In Chapter 3, a data mesh changes how organizations serve data. Each domain team in a data mesh handles serving data to other teams. Teams prepare data for apps, dashboards, and analytics. Domain teams now do both: serve data to others and make their own dashboards and analytics. This [Ch. 9] reorganizes team roles in Chapter 3.
Asked as: "What is benefits of data meshs?"
